title: I Will Survive
coreMove: Reset success to disciplined continuation when the market invalidates the old plan.
sourcePressure: A collapse forces survival metrics: cash, runway, financing tradeoffs, clear communication, execution, reassessment, and another constrained call.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version is perseverance theater: keep believing and refuse to quit.

exampleSpecs.domain: regional food distributor after a restaurant shutdown wave
exampleSpecs.audience: a second-generation operator with freezer inventory and collapsing receivables
exampleSpecs.stakes: payroll, spoilage, lender patience, and customer trust all compete for the same cash
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the operator erases the growth forecast, writes days of cash on the freezer inventory sheet, and chooses the ugly receivables deal that buys three more delivery cycles
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a freezer inventory sheet smudged with thaw-water marks

exampleSpecs.domain: independent dialysis clinic after a reimbursement freeze
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinic administrator deciding how to preserve treatment continuity
exampleSpecs.stakes: patients cannot wait, but staffing and supply contracts no longer fit cash reality
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the administrator crosses out expansion hiring, calls the supply vendor with a staged payment plan, and briefs nurses on the next two-week operating frame
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a treatment chair schedule taped beside an unpaid supply invoice

exampleSpecs.domain: touring orchestra stranded after a sponsor bankruptcy
exampleSpecs.audience: an executive director balancing musician pay, venue deposits, and audience refunds
exampleSpecs.stakes: canceling too much kills trust, but continuing blindly deepens the loss
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director tells section leaders the exact cash gap, names three tour dates that cannot be saved, and assigns one person to renegotiate travel before rumor spreads
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sponsor cancellation letter tucked into a violin case

exampleSpecs.domain: solar installation company after a tax-credit rule change
exampleSpecs.audience: a founder whose signed backlog no longer covers material costs
exampleSpecs.stakes: each completed job may lose money unless terms are renegotiated fast
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the founder has project managers predict cash after each backlog batch, then reveals the material-cost gap and reorders jobs by survivable margin
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a pallet of inverters with a revised tariff notice taped to it

exampleSpecs.domain: county animal shelter after a grant is suspended
exampleSpecs.audience: a shelter director deciding how to keep essential care open
exampleSpecs.stakes: intake, medication, foster capacity, and public trust all compress into a cash clock
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director converts the annual plan into a fourteen-day care plan, posts the facts for staff, and cuts a popular adoption event to preserve medication supply
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a medicine cabinet count sheet beside a postponed event flyer

exampleSpecs.domain: industrial parts importer after a port closure
exampleSpecs.audience: a logistics owner whose customers need parts while containers sit offshore
exampleSpecs.stakes: expedited air freight preserves a few accounts but burns runway
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner ranks customers by survival impact, approves air freight for only two, and sends the same factual delay note to the rest
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a container-tracking screen stuck on vessel waiting outside harbor

skillTargets: recognize when survival has replaced growth as the metric
evaluate runway gained against control and execution costs
distinguish active adaptation from passive endurance

tryThisNowSpec: For one pressured project, replace the success metric with the next survival interval: cash, time, trust, or capacity needed to reach one more disciplined decision.
sourceAnchorsNote: source contains no named anecdote for this chapter
